name: Londonderry
title: Londonderry Ship Gauging: UTM at Foyle Port and Lisahally
description: Thickness gauging at Foyle Port, Lisahally, for bulk carriers, fuel tankers and cruise ships: hold, tank and deck UTM, piping and crack checks on the Foyle.
h1: Ultrasonic Thickness Measurement for Ships on the Foyle at Londonderry
intro: Foyle Port's deep-water terminal at Lisahally, downstream of Londonderry on the River Foyle, is the main harbour for the north-west of Ireland. It is above all a bulk port: fuel, coal, animal feed, fertiliser and plywood arrive on tankers, bulk carriers and general cargo ships, and cruise calls have grown strongly in recent seasons. A discharge lasting days rather than hours gives time to gauge holds, tanks and piping properly. Technicians fly in from India for each job and work on board while the cargo moves.
keywords: bulk carrier hold gauging northern ireland

highlights.p: Bulk carriers bringing feed, fertiliser or coal to the north-west usually stay alongside for days rather than hours. Holds can be gauged one after another as each is emptied and swept, with topside and hopper tanks opened in the order the chief officer can release them.

highlights.h: Fuel tankers on a regular run
highlights.p: Product tankers supplying the region's fuel return to the Foyle on a steady cycle. Deck lines and released deck plating can be measured during one discharge, and the tank structure on a later call when the ship arrives clean or can be made gas-free.

Cruise ships berth at Lisahally, come up to the city-centre quays or anchor off Greencastle and land passengers by tender, depending on size. A day alongside suits engine-room and scrubber piping checks taken as one stage of a pre-docking programme.

port.h: Foyle Port: a river harbour at the head of Lough Foyle
p: Ships bound for Londonderry enter Lough Foyle through the narrow mouth between Magilligan Point and Greencastle, then follow a maintained, buoyed channel across the lough and up the River Foyle. The Londonderry Port and Harbour Commissioners, who trade as Foyle Port, look after that channel and run the harbour, and pilotage and towage are arranged through them and the ship's agent. Commercial shipping left the old city quays for Lisahally in 1993, when the deep-water terminal there was developed, although smaller vessels and some cruise ships still come right up to the city. Outside the channel the lough is shallow, the tidal streams through the entrance narrows run hard, and passages are planned around the tide, so a ship's time at the berth is known some hours ahead rather than left open. That predictability helps when an inspection team has to be waiting on the quay as the ship makes fast.

Lisahally serves a wide hinterland across the north-west of the island, including Donegal on the far side of the border, and its cargo mix reflects a rural region that imports its energy and its farm inputs. Liquid fuels arrive by product tanker for distribution across the area. Bulk carriers and general cargo ships bring animal feed and fertiliser for livestock farming, coal, and plywood for the building trade. Most of the cargo ships are handysize or smaller bulk carriers, multipurpose vessels and short-sea traders, under a wide spread of flags and managers. Cruise traffic has become a second business of real weight: Foyle Port has reported record seasons, with expedition and mid-size ships berthing at Lisahally or in the city and larger ones anchoring in the lough. The port's history runs deep as well; the German U-boat fleet surrendered at Lisahally in May 1945, at the end of the Battle of the Atlantic.

For inspection planning, the Foyle offers time rather than repair facilities. No commercial drydock works on the river today, so dockings for ships in this trade happen elsewhere, most often at Belfast or at yards in Britain and on the Continent. What Lisahally does offer is the length of a bulk discharge, the regularity of the fuel trade and a river berth where work on deck is seldom stopped by sea conditions, even when Atlantic weather is rough beyond the lough. Winter brings westerly and north-westerly gales that can delay a ship at the lough entrance, so a job planned for December or January carries a wider margin in the travel dates than one planned for July. The cruise season runs mainly from spring to autumn, which is also when the quays are busiest, and that affects how an extended stay for gauging is negotiated with the harbour.

facilities.h: Where a ship can be gauged on the Foyle
p: Most gauging on the Foyle happens at the Lisahally terminal while cargo is being worked. The quay is a working bulk berth, so the team coordinates with the stevedores: hold readings are taken behind the grabs once a hold is empty and swept, tank entry follows the ship's enclosed-space permit, and deck work keeps out of the crane's swing. Fuel tankers discharge under tighter rules, with loose equipment and anything that could cause a spark kept away from the manifold, so tanker work alongside concentrates on deck plating, cargo and ballast line runs, vent heads and air pipes that the master releases to the team.

The city-centre berths and the pontoons of the Foyle Port Marina take smaller ships, including cruise ships of modest size, where short in-service checks are realistic within a day's call. A ship waiting in the lough for the tide or for a free berth can be boarded by launch through the agent, but anchorage stays here tend to be short, so the scope has to be small. Anything that needs dry access to the bottom shell, sea chests or rudder means a docking elsewhere; in that case we measure the internal structure on the Foyle call, so that the external work in dock begins from known figures.
list: Lisahally bulk berths — hold, hopper and topside tank gauging on feed, fertiliser and coal carriers during discharges that run over several days.
Lisahally liquid-bulk discharge — deck, cargo-line and ballast-line UT on product tankers within the terminal's permit rules.
Lisahally cruise calls — engine-room, grey-water and scrubber piping on cruise ships alongside for the day.
City-centre quays and Foyle Port Marina — short in-service checks on smaller cruise and passenger vessels lying near the city.
Lough Foyle anchorage — limited launch-borne deck and air-pipe readings on ships waiting for the tide or a berth.
Docking elsewhere — internal structure gauged at Lisahally ahead of a drydock at Belfast or at a yard in Britain.

context.h: Port state control and paperwork for ships calling at Londonderry
p: Londonderry is a UK port, so port state control is the job of the Maritime and Coastguard Agency, which continues to apply the Paris MoU regime through UK law. Bulk carriers and tankers calling at Lisahally are selected on the same risk-based targeting used across the region, and older ships on the bulk trades draw attention to hold frames, hatch covers and coamings, ballast tank coatings and the other structural items that most often lead to detentions. A recent set of thickness readings kept on board lets a master answer an inspector's questions about wastage that is plainly visible on deck or in a hold.

Lough Foyle has an unusual status: the UK and Ireland have never settled where the boundary runs through its waters, and the channel to Lisahally passes close to the Donegal shore on the way in. For the ship, the working regime is the UK one, with Foyle Port running the channel and berths and the MCA carrying out inspections. Britain carried the EU ship recycling rules into its own legislation when it left the EU, and many vessels on these routes also call at Irish or continental ports where the EU regulation requires an Inventory of Hazardous Materials, so the inventory is a document most ships here already hold. Cruise ships meet the widest range of checks, because one itinerary around the island can alternate between UK and EU ports.

jobs.h: Typical thickness gauging jobs at Londonderry
jobs.p: Work at Lisahally is shaped by the cargo. Bulk carriers give the longest windows and the most hold access, tankers give regular but restricted ones, and cruise ships give a single day. Because the river has no drydock, most of our jobs here are either in-service condition gauging for the owner or advance gauging that feeds a docking somewhere else, and the scope is agreed with the superintendent before the ship sails for the Foyle. Readings are sent in the class TM format, so the yard that carries out the docking and the surveyor who attends it can use them without measuring the same plates twice.
list: Hold and topside tank gauging on a handysize bulk carrier discharging animal feed, worked hold by hold over the stay.
Pre-docking readings on a fertiliser carrier's ballast tanks and double bottom, ahead of an intermediate survey at Belfast.
Deck plating, cargo lines and vent heads on a product tanker during a fuel discharge, with the tanks gauged on a later clean call.
Hatch cover and coaming gauging on a general cargo ship delivering plywood, after damage was reported at the loading port.
Scrubber wash-water and sea-water piping on a cruise ship during a day alongside at Lisahally.

logistics: City of Derry Airport at Eglinton is the nearest airport but has few routes, so long-haul arrivals usually come into Belfast International or Dublin and continue by road. Arriving through Dublin means clearing Irish immigration first; the land border into Northern Ireland has no routine checks, yet the team still needs valid UK permission for a job at Lisahally, so we choose the route to match the visas held. UK visas are applied for as soon as the call is fixed, and gate access to the terminal and any launch for the lough are arranged through the ship's agent.

faqs.q: Is there a drydock on the River Foyle?
faqs.a: No commercial drydock operates on the Foyle today. Ships trading to Lisahally go to Belfast, or to yards in Britain or on the Continent, when they need a docking. What can be done on the Foyle is to gauge holds, tanks, decks and piping during a cargo call, so the superintendent goes into the docking with a steel estimate instead of waiting for the yard to find the wastage once the ship is in.

faqs.q: Can holds be gauged while a bulk carrier discharges at Lisahally?
faqs.a: Yes, in sequence. Once a hold is empty and the residues have been swept or washed out, the team works the frames, side shell, hopper plating and tank top while the next hold is still discharging. Coal and fertiliser residues make cleaning before gauging especially important, so we agree with the chief officer which holds will be ready on each day of the stay.

faqs.q: Can cruise ships anchored off Greencastle be gauged?
faqs.a: Rarely in a useful way. A ship anchored off Greencastle is landing passengers by tender, the stay is short and an inspection team boarding by launch competes with the passenger operation. Gauging makes more sense on calls when the same ship berths at Lisahally or in the city, where the team can come aboard from the quay and spend the day on engine-room and scrubber piping.

faqs.q: Does winter weather affect an inspection at Lisahally?
faqs.a: It affects the arrival more than the work. Westerly gales can hold a ship outside the lough or slow its passage up the channel, and the tide decides when it can reach the berth. Once the ship is alongside at Lisahally, work on deck and in tanks carries on in most weather. For winter jobs we keep a margin in the travel plan and confirm the berthing time with the agent the day before.
